set.hook: Alain Passard's three-star on rue de Varenne, all-vegetable since July 2025 but for honey from his hives.
set.why: Passard took over the address from his old boss Alain Senderens, whose L'Archestrate had stood there, and renamed it L'Arpège. In 2001 he dropped red meat; in July 2025 he dropped every animal product except his own honey, and the 2026 MICHELIN guide still lists the house among the nine three-star tables in Paris. What arrives comes from his three kitchen gardens, picked daily and driven in, so the menu shifts with the week rather than the season.

set.hook: Arnaud Donckele's sauce-first tasting room over the Seine at Cheval Blanc, three stars since 2022.
set.why: The room opened inside Cheval Blanc, the hotel cut out of the old Samaritaine store, and about six months later, in March 2022, MICHELIN gave it all three stars at once. Donckele numbers his sauces like perfumes and builds each menu backwards from them: the langoustine or turbot arrives as the thing that carries a broth, a vinaigrette or a jus. The 2026 guide kept the three stars, and a June 2026 review on Trois Etoiles shows the menus still running.

set.hook: Bruno Verjus's two-star counter by the Marché d'Aligre, closing for good after service on 22 December 2026.
set.why: Verjus announced in an Instagram video that Table will serve for the last time on 22 December 2026, thirteen years after it opened in April 2013. His reason, quoted by Gault&Millau, is that 'fine dining is dead': he no longer wants a cooking whose price shuts most people out, and he plans to write, in Greece. Until then it keeps its two MICHELIN stars and its single daily Couleur du jour menu, which put it at No. 3 in the world in 2024.

set.hook: A walnut counter in the 11th where binchotan yakitori and hand-rolled pasta share one tasting menu.

set.hook: Guy Savoy's six salons in the old royal mint on the Seine, two MICHELIN stars and La Liste's joint No. 1.
set.why: Savoy trained three years with the Troisgros brothers in Roanne, opened on rue Duret in 1980, and in 2015 moved into the first floor of the Monnaie de Paris, where coins were struck for the kings. MICHELIN took his third star in 2023 after twenty-one years; La Liste has still put him at No. 1 for nine straight years. The artichoke and black-truffle soup, with a truffle brioche to drag through it, is the plate Gault&Millau's 2026 review still sends you for.

set.hook: The gilded 1901 buffet above Gare de Lyon's Hall 1, with lamb carved from a trolley under 41 painted panels.
set.why: The buffet was built for the 1900 Exposition Universelle and opened the next year; painters of the day covered its walls and ceilings with views of the cities the Paris-Lyon-Méditerranée line ran to, and in 1972 the room was listed as a historic monument. The station caterer SSP later paid for a full restoration of the gilding, stucco and canvases. Since 2018 the menu has been curated by Michel Rostang: lamb carved at the trolley, crêpes Suzette flamed at the table, a rum baba.

set.hook: The Cirque d'Hiver's 1902 bar, ringed by a clown-tile frieze; now a natural-wine bistro serving brain in dashi
set.why: The circus next door sent its clowns and acrobats here to drink; the Sarreguemines ceramic frieze of clowns that wraps the room is why it was listed as a historic monument in 1995. Sven Chartier and Ewen Lemoigne of Saturne took it over in 2014 and hired Sota Atsumi, whose poached calf's brain in cold dashi, added in 2014, has outlived his own departure in 2019 to stay on a card that otherwise keeps changing.

set.hook: The 1997 Faidherbe bistro of steak au poivre, gougères and Paris-Brest, booked by phone only.
set.why: Bertrand Auboyneau left finance to open the bistro in 1997 with his wife Gwenaëlle Cadoret, and built its cellar on growers' wines; he later added Le 6 Paul Bert a few doors down. The steak au poivre is the reason most people call: a thick cut crusted in cracked pepper, sauced with cognac and cream, with frites. Dorie Greenspan liked it enough to adapt it for her book Around My French Table.

set.hook: Stéphane Jégo's loud Basque canteen on rue Malar, famous for one shared bowl of rice pudding.
set.why: Jégo cooked for a decade with Yves Camdeborde at La Régalade, then in 2002 took over this old Basque canteen near the Invalides. His riz au lait arrives as a single big bowl for the table, with salted-butter caramel and house nougatine on the side to fold in yourself; Time Out has printed the recipe. In autumn and winter the board turns to game. Gault&Millau's 2026 review keeps it at 13/20 but finds the cooking a little on autopilot.

set.hook: A 1964 weekday bistro on rue du Mail with a handwritten menu, salade lyonnaise and calf's liver.
set.why: Georges opened the room in 1964 and his family kept it for nearly fifty years; in 2010 Jean-Gabriel de Bueil and Dominique Paul bought it on the promise to change nothing, and they have not. The menu is still written by hand, the salade lyonnaise still comes as a bowl to share, and the chicken is pan-roasted to the season. Gilles Pudlowski went back in March 2026 and found the decor untouched.

creme.title: Three stars, three answers
creme.story: Paris went into the 2026 MICHELIN guide with nine three-star tables, and L'Ambroisie, the oldest of them, came out with two. Three of the nine are in this lane, each answering the question of luxury differently. L'Arpège, Alain Passard's room on the site of his old boss's L'Archestrate, struck every animal product but its own honey from the menu in July 2025 and kept its stars. Plénitude, inside Cheval Blanc on the Seine, went from nothing to three in March 2022 on the strength of Arnaud Donckele's numbered sauces. Kei, near the Louvre, made Kei Kobayashi in 2020 the first Japanese-born chef to hold three stars in France.
creme.where: L'Arpège on rue de Varenne; Plénitude on Quai du Louvre; Kei on rue Coq-Héron

produce.title: The day's market, cooked
produce.story: These kitchens are written from what came in that morning rather than from a fixed repertoire. Table, opened in 2013 by Bruno Verjus, a former critic who started cooking in his fifties, serves one daily menu at a counter by the Marché d'Aligre; it reached No. 3 in the world in 2024 and will serve for the last time on 22 December 2026. Datil, Manon Fleury's room in the 3rd since 2023, opens on a broth of peelings and won a MICHELIN Green Star in March 2026. Le Rigmarole, in the 11th, cooks over Japanese binchotan and rolls Italian pasta by hand at the same walnut counter.
produce.where: Table by Bruno Verjus by the Marché d'Aligre; Datil on rue des Gravilliers; Le Rigmarole on rue du Grand Prieuré

grand.title: Rooms older than menus
grand.story: In these three the room came first and the cooking has changed hands around it. Le Grand Véfour has traded under the Palais-Royal arcades since 1784; Guy Martin left at the end of 2025, and on 12 May 2026 Paris Society reopened it with Bruno Doucet carving lamb at the table and a 150-seat garden terrace. Guy Savoy moved in 2015 into the first floor of the Monnaie de Paris, the old royal mint; MICHELIN took one star in 2023, while La Liste still ranks it first. Le Train Bleu, above Gare de Lyon since 1901, has had its painted walls listed as a monument since 1972.
grand.where: Le Grand Véfour on rue de Beaujolais; Guy Savoy on Quai de Conti; Le Train Bleu on Place Louis-Armand

neo.title: The 11th's small plates
neo.story: The neo-bistro, a short menu of ambitious cooking in a plain room at bistro prices, took root in the 11th in the 2010s. Septime opened on rue de Charonne in 2011, won a star in 2014 and became the template; its founding chef Bertrand Grébaut died in July 2026, aged 44, and the room cooks on. Le Servan, opened in 2014 by Tatiana and Katia Levha in an old bar on rue Saint-Maur, was Le Fooding's best bistro of 2015 and serves blood-sausage wontons. Clown Bar, the Cirque d'Hiver's 1902 bar, was taken over in 2014 by the Saturne team and kept its listed clown frieze.
neo.where: Septime on rue de Charonne; Le Servan on rue Saint-Maur; Clown Bar on rue Amelot

bistro.title: Bistros that kept the script
bistro.story: The classic Paris bistro runs on a short list: terrine, steak, liver, rice pudding, a phone you have to call. Bistrot Paul Bert, opened in 1997 by Bertrand Auboyneau, a former finance man, built its name on steak au poivre and growers' wine and still takes bookings by phone only. Chez L'Ami Jean, Stéphane Jégo's Basque canteen near the Invalides since 2002, is known for a single shared bowl of riz au lait and autumn game. Chez Georges, on rue du Mail since 1964, still hands out a menu written by hand and closes every weekend and through August.
bistro.where: Bistrot Paul Bert on rue Paul Bert; Chez L'Ami Jean on rue Malar; Chez Georges on rue du Mail

_notes: All 15 venues checked from WebSearch extracts only (about 33 searches, no page reads). Status: 9 confirmed (L'Arpège, Plénitude, Kei, Datil, Le Grand Véfour, Guy Savoy, Septime, Chez L'Ami Jean, Chez Georges), 1 time_limited (Table by Bruno Verjus, last service 22 Dec 2026), 5 unverified (Le Rigmarole, Le Train Bleu, Le Servan, Clown Bar, Bistrot Paul Bert): for the last four the only 2026-dated evidence is the Mes Prestiges listing (reviewed May 2026) or aggregators, and Mes Prestiges proved unreliable (it gives Guy Savoy both two and three stars for 2026, names Sota Atsumi at Clown Bar seven years after he left, and claims stars or Bibs for Le Servan, Paul Bert and L'Ami Jean that no MICHELIN source confirms). No closures found apart from Table's announced one. Big changes: (1) Table by Bruno Verjus closes for good on 22 December 2026 (Gault&Millau, Sortiraparis Sept 2026). (2) Septime's chef-founder Bertrand Grébaut died in early July 2026, aged 44; the restaurant is cooking on (Gault&Millau 2026), current head chef not found; person/verdict need rewording. (3) Le Rigmarole: Gilles Pudlowski's March 2023 list of star removals includes it; the old 'one star retained 2026' is dropped. (4) Le Grand Véfour now has Gault&Millau 14/20 'Table de Chef' (2026), contradicting the old 'unrated'. (5) Guy Savoy menu now EUR 740 (Yonder Jan 2026), not ~490. World's 50 Best: the brief says the 2026 list was published in June 2026; the 50 Best site says the 2026 ranking is unveiled on 4 November 2026 in Lima. All ranks printed (Plénitude 14, Table 8, Septime 40, Arpège 45) are 2025 and labelled so. MICHELIN 2026: nine Paris three-stars incl. Arpège, Plénitude, Kei (JDS/LesRestos palmarès, ceremony 16 March 2026); L'Ambroisie lost its third. Guy Savoy's two stars in 2026 rest on Yonder (Jan 2026), not a MICHELIN extract. Datil's Green Star 2026 confirmed (Sortiraparis, Pudlowski); its red-star year is disputed (2024 vs 2025). Table's address in the record contains a word banned by the brief; I did not set or repeat the address, and the lane 'where' places it by the Marché d'Aligre. Verdict fields not rewritten (outside this brief) but flagged in corrections where wrong: Arpège egg, Rigmarole star, Grand Véfour 'unrated', Guy Savoy price, Septime chef. Plénitude: no 2026 price found (450/390 vs 480/445). Train Bleu head chef disputed (Samir Balia vs Jean-Pierre Hocquet) and Rostang start (2018 vs 2023).
